entry.title: What If It Was 200°F for 10 Years ?

media:group.media:title: What If It Was 200°F for 10 Years ?
media:group.media:description:
What if the Sun got brighter one morning — and stayed that way for ten years? By 3 PM it's 200°F (93°C) in the air. Power lines sag, air conditioners quit, the coasts go silent.
You're a lineman in a small Nevada desert town. A hydrogeologist named Tess, with a thermometer and a green notebook, leads you to the one place that stays cold: an old silver mine, 300 feet under a hill.
The endless heat is our "what if." The rest we kept real: why dry heat is survivable and humid heat isn't, why air conditioners stop working, how deep rock remembers the average of the year, why cold air drains out of a mine like water from a bucket, what heat stroke does and how to treat it — and why, after ten years, the rain had to come.
What would you have written on the last page of her notebook? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: You Built a Bunker to Last 5 Years. You Stayed for 50

media:group.media:title: You Built a Bunker to Last 5 Years. You Stayed for 50
media:group.media:description:
You built a bunker for one person and five years. Then the war never ended — and you stayed underground for fifty.
A bunker survival story animation about one man, one room under a barn, and the war that kept going above him. Armies dig trenches across your field, every farmhouse for thirty miles burns, and nuclear war turns the country into a map nobody can read. Below, a single shelter slowly grows into an underground village of 34 people — a mechanic named Nolan, a woman named Lena, a son born twelve feet under the ground. And for fifty years, nobody touches your hatch.
Everything about how the bunker works is kept real: how fallout fades, how long diesel, filters and LED bulbs actually last, how much heat a crowded shelter makes, how you grow food with no sun, and what fifty years underground does to a body and a mind.
Would you have opened the hatch? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: What If It Was -100°C for 10 Years?

media:group.media:title: What If It Was -100°C for 10 Years?
media:group.media:description:
What if it was −100°C (−148°F) for 10 years — and you had to survive it? In this animated survival story, the polar vortex collapses, your city freezes in a single night, and the cold never leaves. How long would you last?
You're the super of an old apartment building. You drain the pipes before they burst, build a stove from a steel drum, and burn the building one apartment at a time. A young mine hoist operator named Iris walks toward your chimney smoke. Then one night, someone knocks on the heating pipe… and you knock back. What follows is ten years of extreme cold survival: a robbery that takes your fire, a nine-mile walk across a frozen city, and a salt mine 650 feet underground where the temperature never drops.
The never-ending winter is our "what if." Everything else is real science of cold survival: • Why mercury thermometers stop working at −39°C • Why ordinary steel shatters in arctic cold — and copper doesn't • Why wet wood plugs a chimney with ice • Why frozen food never spoils • Why the frost line goes deeper into the ground every year • Why a deep salt mine stays around +20°C (68°F) all year round
If you like winter survival stories, arctic survival, "how long would you survive" scenarios and animated what-if videos, this one is for you.
💬 If those five men had never taken your fire — when would you have walked away from it on your own? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: You Have 30 Days Before Nuclear War. Can You Survive?

media:group.media:title: You Have 30 Days Before Nuclear War. Can You Survive?
media:group.media:description:
At 2:14 in the morning, your best friend calls from an Air Force base forty miles away. Two sentences: "Thirty days. Get underground." Then he hangs up.
A real bunker takes four months. You have thirty days, $38,000 and a family that thinks you've lost your mind. You borrow $190,000, haul a steel pipe four hundred miles, hit groundwater at eleven feet, drive nine hundred miles for an air filter and drill a well that comes up dry. Every week something breaks. Every week you fall further behind.
The war, the countries and the town are fiction. The engineering is real: why shipping containers cave in underground, why three feet of dirt beats a steel door, why a bunker entrance needs a 90-degree turn, why deep well water stays clean, and why body heat can be more dangerous than radiation in a crowded shelter.
Someone is knocking on the hatch. Do you open it? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: What If It Never Stopped Raining for 10 Years?

media:group.media:title: What If It Never Stopped Raining for 10 Years?
media:group.media:description:
What if the rain never stopped? Not for a week. Not for a year. For ten years.
You live on the 24th floor of a tower by the bay. On day six, the last evacuation bus leaves without you. What follows is a decade of catching rain from the roof, keeping warm without power, finding food that doesn't need the sun, dodging bull sharks in the streets, and watching saltwater eat your building from the inside.
The endless rain is fiction. The survival is real: atmospheric rivers, the Great Flood of 1862, the Year Without a Summer, bull sharks in floodwater, rebar corrosion, carbon monoxide, safe water. On day six, with that line around the corner, what would you have done? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: The Zombies Were TOO SMART… Surviving 10 Years on a Farm (Full Movie)

media:group.media:title: The Zombies Were TOO SMART… Surviving 10 Years on a Farm (Full Movie)
media:group.media:description:
A zombie apocalypse survival story: a father holds his Iowa farm for 10 years, waiting for his wife and daughter to come home. Animated survival story told in the second person — YOU are the one living it.
The outbreak hits on a normal morning. Your wife Anna is driving your daughter Mia to school in Ridley. One phone call, then the lines go dead. The roads are blocked, the town is burning, and all you have left is a farm, a well, a windmill, a dog named Duke — and a message you leave for them: STAY AT THE FARM. WE'LL COME TO YOU.
For ten years you survive alone. You dig a ditch around the farm, fix the windmill, build a dam, ration water, food and shotgun shells. You fight drought, blizzards and a pack led by a big one in an orange vest. You learn how they think: they learn your doors, they copy voices, they wait. And every evening, at the edge of the east woods, something stands and watches your house. It never attacks. Nothing ever comes from the east.
In year seven, a girl walks up to your gate in the middle of the night and says: "Dad?"
Would you have opened the gate?

entry.title: What If You Were the Last Human on Earth for 10 Years?

media:group.media:title: What If You Were the Last Human on Earth for 10 Years?
media:group.media:description:
What if you had the entire world to yourself for 10 years? Explore the psychological journey of total isolation in this narrative experiment.
This story follows one man as he navigates a decade of absolute solitude. From his first days behind the wheel to the quiet routines of a life lived in a vacant world, we track the mental progression of a man who suddenly finds himself without another soul in sight. It is a look at what happens when your only company is a list of aspirations and the silence of a city at sunset.
As the years pass, the narrative shifts from simple survival to a strange, mysterious conclusion. We analyze the reality of long-term isolation and the weight of being the last person remaining. Whether you are interested in a deep character study or a hypothetical world to yourself scenario, this animation covers the full arc of the experience.
What would you do if you were the last person on Earth for a decade? Tell me in the comments if you could handle the silence. Subscribe for more psychological survival stories and hypothetical scenarios.

entry.title: You Spent 10 Years in a Bunker. You Only Needed 5.

media:group.media:title: You Spent 10 Years in a Bunker. You Only Needed 5.
media:group.media:description:
What would it actually take to survive 10 years in a bunker after a nuclear war?
October 14. Omaha disappears in a flash 60 miles away, and you have about an hour before the fallout reaches your farm. Your only chance is the shelter your grandfather built under the barn in 1962 — a concrete room 12 feet underground, with an old logbook, a hand pump and a wall of wheat buckets.
You go down. Then you stay down. For 3,650 days.
In this animated survival story you'll see, step by step, how a real fallout shelter keeps you alive: how radiation fades with time, how you filter air, store water, make power and ration food — and what happens when the supplies, the batteries and the filters start running out.
But the hardest part isn't the bunker. It's the voices. A stranger begging at the air pipe. A man named Dutch who wants what you have. A fire on top of your hatch. And every Sunday, the same knock on the steel: shave and a haircut… two bits.
Would you have answered the knock? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: 30 Days Trapped on the 40th Floor During a Zombie Apocalypse

media:group.media:title: 30 Days Trapped on the 40th Floor During a Zombie Apocalypse
media:group.media:description:
A zombie outbreak hits while you're trapped on the 40th floor of a hotel. This is a zombie apocalypse survival story told day by day: can you survive 30 days?
Your phone beeps at 5:26 AM: "Stay indoors. Do not open your door for anyone." Then something starts scratching at your door. The zombie outbreak has begun, the elevators are dead, and the only way out is 40 floors down.
This zombie survival story follows your zombie outbreak survival from day 1 to day 30, with four strangers: Tom the security guard, Mara the night nurse, Ray the businessman, and Leo, a 12-year-old boy waiting for his dad. Day by day survival on the 40th floor means counting every liter of water, every can of food and every battery.
The rules of this zombie apocalypse: 1. Stairwell doors lock behind you. 2. They go toward noise and light. 3. They remember where they saw you. 4. Never walk the same way twice.
It's a stick figure animation and survival animation in one: a stickman survival story about how to survive a zombie apocalypse when you can't run, can't call for help and can't turn on a light. If you like zombie animation, apocalypse survival and "what would you do" scenarios, this zombie outbreak 30 days challenge is for you.
